# Draft:Independent reviews in the United Kingdom__disambig_2

Independent reviews in the United Kingdom, sometimes also known as independent policy reviews, are a type of public inquiry that involve evaluations or investigations led by individuals or panels external to government departments or public bodies. They are typically commissioned to provide impartial analysis and recommendations on policy, regulatory, or operational issues, and are similar but distinct from statutory public inquiries, which are typically regulated by the Inquiries Act 2005 and The Inquiry Rules 2006.

In the UK, several different types of public inquiries are carried out. They can be broadly grouped into being either statutory, in which case they are usually held under and regulated by the Inquiries Act 2005 and the Inquiries Rules 2006, or non-statutory in nature. Although statutory public inquiries are more common, statutory and non-statutory public inquiries each have their own advantages and disadvantages. For instance, non-statutory public inquiries have greater procedural flexibility, while statutory public inquiries are able to legally compel evidence and gather it under oath. Therefore, the exact type of public inquiry used will depend on the scope of the inquiry and the nature of the topic it investigates.
There are a few different types of non-statutory public inquiries, including Royal Commissions and non-statutory ad-hoc inquiries. Although the different types of non-statutory public inquiries are all the same in not having their processes defined in legislation, they still differ in other ways. For example, inquiries carried out by a committee of the UK Privy Council, such as the Iraq Inquiry, are able to see classified information the government would not otherwise make available. Moreover, Royal Commissions generally investigate broader policy or societal issues rather than specific incidents or concerns.

Notable examples
Lammy Review
The Lammy Review was commissioned in January 2016 by Prime Minister David Cameron and the Ministry of Justice and led by MP David Lammy over an 18‑month period, examining every stage of the criminal justice process via calls for evidence, roundtables, site visits, and data analysis. It found stark racial disparities in arrests, sentencing, and custody, identifying opaque sentencing, over‑representation in remand, and lack of trust as key factors. The review made 35 recommendations, including public sentencing explanations, deferred prosecutions, and record sealing, most of which the government adopted by creating a Race and Ethnicity Board and embedding changes in policy. While praised for its rigour and data transparency, campaigners note persistent disparities, and call for full implementation.
Ockenden Review
The Ockenden Review, commissioned in 2017 by Health Secretary, Jeremy Hunt, and led by Donna Ockenden, investigated maternity care at Shrewsbury and Telford Hospital NHS Trust following concerns from bereaved families. The review examined over 1,400 cases, identifying systemic failures such as staffing shortages, inadequate training, poor governance, and a culture that failed to listen to women. It issued 15 national Immediate and Essential Actions and over 60 Trust-specific recommendations aimed at improving maternity safety. The findings were widely praised for their thoroughness, prompting NHS England to implement a Safer Maternity Care strategy, though campaigners and MPs continue to warn that sustained cultural change and full accountability are still needed.
Browne Review
The Browne review was commissioned in November 2009 by Business Secretary, Peter Mandelson, and chaired by Lord Browne to examine university fees and student finance amid concerns over sustainability and access. It gathered evidence through public hearings, over 150 written submissions, sector and student consultations, and data analysis in 2009–10. The review recommended removing the £3,290 fee cap in favour of a variable‑fee model tied to graduate earnings, raising the repayment threshold to £21,000, and establishing an independent higher education council. The government broadly welcomed the findings, raising the cap in 2012 and enhancing access measures, although critics warned of increased student debt and potential quality‑undermining effects.
